content.title: Graphing Linear Inequalities in the Coordinate Plane
content.overview: This lesson explains how to represent the solution set of a linear inequality in two variables by drawing boundary lines and identifying shaded regions in the Cartesian coordinate system. Mastering this skill is essential for solving graph identification problems and systems of inequalities on the SAT Math section.
learning_objectives: Accurately draw boundary lines based on the inequality symbol (solid or dashed).
Determine the shaded region by substituting test points or observing the inequality direction.
Identify the inequality expression corresponding to a given graph on the coordinate plane.
Understand the geometric meaning of the solution set of a linear inequality in two variables.

sections.title: Drawing the Boundary Line
sections.content: The first step in graphing a linear inequality (such as $y > mx + b$) is to treat it as an equation ($y = mx + b$) and draw the boundary line. The type of line depends on the inequality symbol: if it includes an equal sign ($≤$ or $≥$), use a solid line to indicate that points on the boundary are part of the solution; if it does not include an equal sign ($<$ or $>$), use a dashed line to indicate that points on the boundary are not solutions.

sections.title: Determining the Shaded Region
sections.content:
The solution set of an inequality is a half-plane region. There are two common methods to determine the shading direction: 1. **Test Point Method**: Choose a point not on the boundary line (usually $(0,0)$) and substitute it into the inequality. If the statement is true, shade the side containing that point; if false, shade the opposite side. 2. **Observation Method**: When the inequality is written in the form $y >$ or $y ≥$, shade above the boundary line; when written as $y <$ or $y ≤$, shade below the boundary line.

![Steps to Graph Linear Inequalities in Two Variables](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/0cb9956c-75ea-4cb5-ac4c-363c8fea2e48-1786502038107-344.webp)

worked_examples.question: Represent the solution set of the inequality $2x - 3y ≤ 6$ on the coordinate plane.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Find the intercepts of the boundary line $2x - 3y = 6$. When $x=0$, $y=-2$; when $y=0$, $x=3$. Connect $(0,-2)$ and $(3,0)$. Step 2: Since the symbol is $≤$, draw a solid line. Step 3: Use the test point $(0,0)$. Substituting gives $2(0) - 3(0) ≤ 6$, which simplifies to $0 ≤ 6$. This statement is true, so the shaded region includes the origin, which is the area above and to the left of the boundary line.

common_mistakes: Confusing dashed and solid lines: Forgetting that a dashed line must be used when there is no equal sign.
Incorrect shading direction: Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number to isolate $y$, which makes the observation method fail.
Improper test point selection: Choosing a point that lies exactly on the boundary line, making it impossible to determine the region.
exam_tips: In SAT multiple-choice questions, check whether the boundary line is solid or dashed first to quickly eliminate half of the options.

Check the coefficient of $y$: If the coefficient of $y$ is negative, it is recommended to simplify it to the standard form with $y$ on the left before judging 'above' or 'below', or simply use the test point method to avoid errors.
Vertical lines ($x < a$) and horizontal lines ($y > b$) are special cases: $x < a$ is shaded to the left, and $y > b$ is shaded upward.
content.recap: Representing a linear inequality on the coordinate plane requires: 1. Determining the boundary line position; 2. Deciding between a solid or dashed line based on the presence of an equal sign; 3. Determining the shaded region using a test point or the sign of $y$.

knowledge_claims.content: When representing a linear inequality, if the symbol is $<$ or $>$, the boundary line must be drawn as a dashed line.
When representing a linear inequality, if the symbol is $≤$ or $≥$, the boundary line must be drawn as a solid line.
The solution set of a linear inequality in two variables is represented on the coordinate plane as a half-plane region defined by a boundary line.

The test point method requires selecting a coordinate point not on the boundary line and substituting it into the inequality; if the inequality holds true, the side containing that point is the solution region.
For an inequality in the form $y > mx + b$, the solution region is located above the boundary line.
For an inequality in the form $y < mx + b$, the solution region is located below the boundary line.
If both sides of an inequality are divided by a negative number to isolate $y$, the direction of the inequality sign must be flipped, otherwise the shaded region will be incorrect.
For a vertical boundary line $x = k$, the solution set for $x > k$ is located to the right of the line.
For a horizontal boundary line $y = k$, the solution set for $y < k$ is located below the line.
The origin $(0,0)$ is the most commonly used test point, provided the boundary line does not pass through the origin.
